---
title: "Tidyverse verbs"
subtitle: "Build a transparent analysis dataset one explicit decision at a time."
---

## The six questions

| Question | Verb |
|---|---|
| Which variables do I need? | `select()` |
| Which observations do I need? | `filter()` |
| Which new variables do I need? | `mutate()` |
| In which order? | `arrange()` |
| Within which groups? | `group_by()` |
| Which summary values? | `summarise()` |

## `select()`: choose columns

```r
analysis_data <- patients |>
  select(patient_id, age, treatment, outcome)
```

Useful helpers include `starts_with()`, `ends_with()`, `contains()`, and `everything()`. Explicit names are preferable when the analysis depends on a small prespecified set of variables.

## `filter()`: choose rows

```r
adults <- patients |>
  filter(
    age >= 18,
    treatment %in% c("Intervention", "Usual care"),
    !is.na(outcome)
  )
```

Comma-separated conditions inside `filter()` must all be true. Use `|` for “or” and `&` for “and” when writing compound expressions.

## `mutate()`: create or change variables

```r
prepared_data <- adults |>
  mutate(
    age_decade = age / 10,
    older_adult = age >= 65,
    risk_group = case_when(
      predicted_risk < 0.10 ~ "Lower",
      predicted_risk < 0.20 ~ "Intermediate",
      TRUE ~ "Higher"
    )
  )
```

`if_else()` is ideal for two values; `case_when()` handles several mutually exclusive conditions. Order conditions carefully: R uses the first one that evaluates to true.

## `group_by()` and `summarise()`

```r
group_summary <- prepared_data |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(
    patients = n(),
    mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    outcome_risk = mean(outcome == "Event", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

`group_by()` does not calculate anything by itself. It changes how later verbs behave. Use `.groups = "drop"` when the summary should no longer remain grouped.

## `count()`: concise category counts

```r
patients |>
  count(treatment, outcome, name = "patients")
```

This is equivalent to grouping by the listed variables and counting observations.

## `arrange()`, `rename()` and `distinct()`

```r
patients |>
  rename(age_years = age) |>
  arrange(desc(outcome_score)) |>
  distinct(patient_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

Only remove duplicates after identifying why they exist. Repeated rows may represent legitimate repeated measurements rather than data errors.

## Joining datasets

```r
analysis_data <- patients |>
  left_join(laboratory_results, by = "patient_id")
```

A `left_join()` keeps every row from the first dataset and adds matching values from the second. Before and after joining, check:

- whether the key is unique in each dataset;
- row counts;
- unmatched keys;
- whether one patient can legitimately have several matching records.

Many-to-many joins can multiply rows and silently change the unit of analysis.

## A complete preparation pipeline

```r
analysis_data <- raw_data |>
  select(patient_id, age, treatment, baseline_score, outcome) |>
  filter(age >= 18) |>
  mutate(
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("Usual care", "Intervention")),
    age_decade = age / 10
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(outcome))

glimpse(analysis_data)
count(analysis_data, treatment)
```

::: {.callout-important}
Every `filter()` changes the population represented by the analysis. Record how many observations were removed and why.
:::
